newsitem.title: UK: Saudi, UK ministers steer clear of controversy.
newsitem.headline: Saudi, UK ministers steer clear of controversy.

text.p: Britain and Saudi Arabia, setting aside differences over dissidents, joined forces on Wednesday in voicing concern about Middle East peace and issued a warning to Iraq over sanctions.
Defence Minister Prince Sultan, acting in his capacity as second deputy prime minister, began a two-day visit to Britain by lunching with Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind.
He was also due to hold talks with Prime Minister John Major, Queen Elizabeth and the trade and defence ministers.
"Relations are on an excellent footing," a Foreign Office spokesman said. "The level of the reception speaks for itself."

Yet London's relations with Riyadh have suffered tensions, augmented by veiled Saudi threats that London might lose export business because of bitter criticism of the Saudi royal family by London-based dissident Mohammad al-Masari.
The spokesman said these sore points were not discussed.
"The heat has gone out of the issue. Mr Masari is yesterday's man and the Saudis understand our position," he said. "The matters discussed were international in nature."
Britain is anxious to beat its Western rivals for fresh arms sales to Saudi Arabia.
Officials have been rallying support for British main battle tank (MBT) maker Vickers Plc, competing with French and U.S. companies to supply up to 200 MBTs to the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest arms purchaser, has not indicated when it will place an order but the prince's visit to London follows similar missions to France and the United States.
The Foreign Office spokesman said defence matters would be raised on Thursday. Wednesday's talks focused on diplomacy.
On Middle East peace, Rifkind said Israel's plan to build a new settlement had "soured the positive atmosphere" and stressed that such actions were illegal and risked damaging the process.

"We are both deeply concerned about recent developments," Rifkind said in a statement. "It is vital for the whole region and for the international community that gains made in the peace process are not allowed to slip away."
Rifkind said the two nations had also stressed their continued resolve against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
"Sanctions must remain in place until Iraq complies with all the relevant (U.N.) Security Council resolutions. Sadly, it is hard to see this happening while Saddam remains in power."
He also raised the alarm about Iranian nuclear ambitions.

"We have seen their purchase of Russian submarines in the not too distant past and there is also concern that they may be seeking to advance a nuclear capability," Rifkind said in the House of Commons after his Saudi talks. "So it is necessary to monitor these matters very carefully and to do all within their power dissuade Iran against such a course of action."
